item.title: Optimal design of higher-order interactions for mutual synchronization among three collectively oscillating networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.02589v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many networked dynamical systems consist of interacting subnetworks, each of which can exhibit collective oscillations. Mutual synchronization among such collectively oscillating networks is ubiquitously observed, and its efficient control is an important engineering problem. While control of synchronization has been extensively studied for pairwise interactions, many systems also involve higher-order interactions among three or more subnetworks that cannot be decomposed into independent pairwise couplings. In this study, we investigate the optimization of higher-order internetwork coupling for mutual synchronization among three collectively oscillating networks. Using phase reduction theory for collectively oscillating networks, we reduce the full network dynamics to a two-dimensional system of phase-difference equations, in which the linear stability of the phase-locked state and the rotational property of the phase differences around it are characterized by a higher-order coupling tensor shared by the three networks. We then derive the optimal coupling tensors that maximize either the linear stability or the rotational property for a fixed overall strength of the internetwork coupling. As a numerical example, we consider three collectively oscillating networks, each consisting of four FitzHugh-Nagumo elements coupled in a tree structure, and demonstrate that, compared with a random coupling tensor of the same overall strength, the two types of optimal coupling yield faster convergence to the phase-locked state and stronger rotational motion of the phase differences around it, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Sotaro Kuroiwa, Yuzuru Kato

item.title: Boom-Busty Marketron as a Model of Market Dynamics: How Investor-Market Reflexivity Amplifies Non-Equilibrium
item.description: arXiv:2611.01185v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce the Boom-Busty Marketron, a model of a multi-asset market in which the demand of a single collective investor moves prices and itself depends on market performance. This creates an investor-market reflexive loop in the spirit of Soros's theory. The market state is stationary without being at equilibrium: a non-equilibrium steady state (NESS), with broken detailed balance and a probability current circulating between mispricing, demand and volatility. While stochastic volatility with the leverage effect already breaks detailed balance and makes the market dynamics irreversible, the investor-market loop pushes the market further away from equilibrium. Calibrated to the S\&P 500 from 1996 to 2024 by simulated moments, the model reproduces the stylised facts of returns together with quantitative metrics of the market, including cross-sectional ones, and its return and cycle statistics stay stationary for a century and a half on the 1996--2010 inputs. Its central emergent behaviour is a boom-bust cycle, whose frequency meets the S\&P's within one-sigma ranges. The model also produces a default rate of the order of that of investment-grade issuers, prices inside Fisher Black's factor of two of value, the dumb-money effect of Frazzini and Lamont, and a measurable arrow of time. Standard long-short factors built from its cross section rotate through the cycle, and so do its industry groups along the defensive axis.
item.dc:creator: Igor Halperin

item.title: Beliefs in feedback: Factored representations of interacting agents in transformers
item.description: arXiv:2611.02047v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Complex systems, from ecosystems to brains, are usually modeled as modular components coupled through feedback rather than as indivisible wholes. Can a transformer trained on the joint behavior of a group of interacting agents be understood in the same way? In this work, we develop a computational-mechanics framework to study agents interacting in feedback loops. We formally prove that any joint stochastic process can be presented as resulting from the behavior of agents interacting in feedback, and the resulting process is generated by a hidden Markov model whose Bayesian beliefs factorize into separate components per agent. Furthermore, our experiments show that transformers trained on such feedback sequences make use of this separability, disentangling the beliefs about the underlying factors into separate subspaces of their residual stream. This representation is found to scale linearly (instead of exponentially) with the number of agents. Moreover, interventions show that these representations are causally efficacious, allowing for targeted steering of individual agents' beliefs by selectively inserting counterfactuals. However, coarse-graining the behavior is found to disrupt the factorization, and can force a higher-dimensional representation. Together, the results establish both the dimensional advantage of a factorized representation and the ability of transformers to exploit it, laying the groundwork for investigating traces of compositional predictive architecture in pretrained models.
item.dc:creator: David A. Ehrlich, Manuel Baltieri, Fernando E. Rosas, Alexander B. Boyd

item.title: When will androids outnumber humans?
item.description: arXiv:2611.03242v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Humanoid robots are increasingly discussed not only as machines but also as a potential technological population. We develop a nonlinear population-dynamical framework to examine their possible diffusion relative to humans, without assuming that large-scale adoption or numerical crossover is inevitable. The human population $H(t)$ is calibrated to the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024 median trajectory. The android population $A(t)$ is represented through the normalized stock $a=A/A_s$. A conventional, human-organized manufacturing and adoption channel is calibrated to a conditional scenario spanning approximately $10^4$ humanoids in 2025 to $10^9$ in 2050 and follows $\dot a=(q_M+r_Ma)\exp(K_Ma^\gamma)$. We separately introduce a hypothetical autonomous channel in which installed androids contribute materially to producing additional androids. Under the minimal canonical TZ closure, the corresponding production--feedback number is $\mathcal{P}(a)=(r_A/\delta_A)\exp(K_Ra)$, where $r_A$ is the gross robot-mediated production coefficient, $\delta_A$ the retirement rate, and $K_R$ the autonomous feedback parameter. This channel is locally self-amplifying if and only if $\mathcal{P}>1$, whereas numerical human--android parity, $A=H$, is a separate cumulative condition. Global uncertainty analysis shows that crossover dates remain strongly scenario-dependent, while the production--feedback threshold is more robust. An extreme early-autonomy stress test can produce parity by 2050, but this represents a conditional dynamical boundary rather than a technological forecast.
item.dc:creator: Alessio Zaccone, Thomas Tunstall, Jesse H. Ausubel

item.title: Solving Stochastic Inverse Problems in Embedding Space
item.description: arXiv:2506.11796v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Solving an inverse problem consists in finding the unknown parameters of a system from observations. This task is particularly challenging when observations have a strong stochastic component, producing diverse yet equivalent patterns. Self-organizing systems are a notable case: simple local rules can generate complex stochastic patterns. Many natural systems rely on such processes, making self-organization central to understanding natural phenomena. Inverse methods based on direct comparison of observed values struggle in this setting, as such comparisons cannot capture feature similarities between variable outcomes; as a result, the loss fails to meaningfully inform the optimizer. In this work, we show that the difficulty posed by stochasticity in observable patterns can be overcome by reformulating the inverse problem in an embedding space. By mapping stochastic patterns onto an invariant embedding space, where equivalent patterns have similar representations, we can effectively recover unknown causal parameters without the need for handcrafted objective functions or heuristics. We show that embedding models trained on large image datasets produce robust representations that capture these invariances. We evaluate the method on three self-organizing systems: a physical, a biological, and a social one; namely, a reaction-diffusion system, a model of embryonic development, and an agent-based model of social segregation. We show that the method reliably recovers parameters despite stochasticity in the pattern outcomes. We further apply the method to real biological patterns, highlighting its potential as a tool for both theorists and experimentalists to investigate the dynamics underlying complex stochastic pattern formation.
item.dc:creator: Elias Najarro, Nicolas Bessone, Sebastian Risi

item.title: How Withheld Punishment Sustains Anti-Democratic Behavior in an Evolutionary Game
item.description: arXiv:2512.06245v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Democratic backsliding is often framed as a contest between defenders and disruptors of democratic institutions. That framing can miss a third response, withholding punishment from disruptors while penalizing defenders who confront them. We model the three responses as strategies in an evolutionary game, track their shares with replicator dynamics, and assume defenders beat disruptors head-to-head but have a payoff disadvantage among non-punishers even when disruptors are absent. If the third response cannot spread among disruptors, a payoff condition draws the population toward the classical May--Leonard heteroclinic cycle, a rock--paper--scissors succession in which disruption repeatedly becomes rare, then widespread. If that response can, a threshold on its payoff advantage over disruptors determines whether all three coexist or defenders alone vanish. In finite-population simulations, sustained resurgence requires reintroducing lost strategies. Our contribution is to show how two separately documented political tendencies, if combined, can sustain disruption despite defenders' head-to-head advantage over disruptors.
item.dc:creator: Chad M. Topaz

item.title: Early warning signals for synchronization transitions from partial observations
item.description: arXiv:2608.28320v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Anticipating the onset of collective synchronization is important in many networked systems, yet observing every oscillator is often impractical. We investigate whether synchronization transitions can be detected from a small set of monitored, or sentinel, nodes. Using a stochastic Kuramoto model on networks, we numerically compare three early warning signals: the local order parameter, its temporal variance, and the variance of individual oscillator phases after removing their mean rotational trends. We also compare sentinel-selection strategies based on node dynamics, degree, and random sampling. We show that, under partial observation, the local order parameter and the variance of detrended phases provide substantially stronger warning signals than the variance of the local order parameter. Selecting nodes according to their dynamical behavior near the transition consistently improves performance over other sentinel-selection methods. With only $\lfloor\ln N\rfloor$ dynamically selected sentinels, two success indicators approach the performance obtained by observing all $N$ nodes. These results demonstrate that synchronization transitions can be anticipated from sparse observations when the warning signal and monitored nodes are chosen appropriately.
item.dc:creator: Yusuke Kato, Naoki Masuda

item.title: Equilibria of Replicator Dynamics in Quantum Games
item.description: arXiv:quant-ph/0106135v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We analyse two-population replicator dynamics for asymmetric $2\times2$ games implemented with the Marinatto--Weber (MW) identity/bit-flip protocol. The effective payoff matrices are explicit convex combinations of relabelled classical matrices. Consequently, the dynamics depends on the initial state only through its four computational-basis probabilities: quantum phases, coherences and entanglement cannot be distinguished from classical shared randomness by the payoffs or trajectories in this protocol. At each pure-strategy vertex, the local eigenvalues equal the negatives of the corresponding unilateral payoff advantages; a vertex is asymptotically stable precisely when it is a strict Nash equilibrium, and thus an evolutionarily stable strategy pair in the asymmetric-game sense. Explicit examples show how varying the initial distribution changes which vertex is stable. When an isolated interior rest point exists, it is a saddle or a nonlinear centre according to the sign of the product of the classical payoff cross-differences; the sign cannot change under the MW mapping, although the point can enter or leave the strategy square. We give all four vertex-stability conditions explicitly in a single table, obtain a closed-form logistic solution on the parity-balanced hyperplane $S=0$, classify the degenerate cases, and give a first integral for the nondegenerate flow. All results concern the MW payoff protocol and its classically simulable family of bimatrix games; none constitutes evidence of an inherently quantum evolutionary advantage.
item.dc:creator: Azhar Iqbal, A. H. Toor
